    Content from Shotgun metagenomics data to study the microbiome

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is the human gut microbiome and how can we study it with sequencing?
    • How does shotgun metagenomics differ from marker-gene (16S rRNA) sequencing?
    • What is the difference between taxonomic and functional profiling?
    • Which dataset will we use in this workshop, and how do we obtain it?

    Objectives

    • Understand the general concepts of the human gut microbiome
    • Distinguish shotgun metagenomics from marker-gene sequencing
    • Explain the difference between taxonomic and functional profiling
    • Map the main stages from FASTQ files to biological interpretation
    • Describe the workshop dataset and metadata
    • Download the workshop dataset and verify its integrity

    The human gut microbiome

    Shotgun metagenomics and marker-gene sequencing

    • Marker-gene sequencing amplifies and sequences one gene region (e.g. 16S rRNA, ITS).
    • Shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA in the sample.

    Taxonomic and functional profiling

    • Taxonomic profiling: which organisms are present and their abundance.
    • Functional profiling: which genes and metabolic pathways are present and their abundance.

    The workshop dataset

    5 simulated human gut metagenomes from Sun, Huang et al. (2021), with paired-end reads, ground-truth abundance tables and sample metadata. The true composition of each sample is known.

    First look at the reads

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    BASH 

    # number of reads in a file (lines / 4)
# PENDING TO WRITE CODE
    Key Points
    • Shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA in a sample.
    • Taxonomic profiling describes which organisms are present; functional profiling describes their genes and pathways.
    • The workshop uses 5 simulated gut metagenomes with a known composition.

    Content from Reproducible workflows with Nextflow and nf-core

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Why is reproducibility a challenge in bioinformatics?
    • What are Nextflow and nf-core, and how do they help?
    • How do I connect to a Nectar instance and check that the software is available?
    • How do I prepare the input files needed by nf-core/taxprofiler and nf-core/funcprofiler?

    Objectives

    • Understand reproducibility in bioinformatics
    • Explain what Nextflow is and why it is useful

    Reproducibility in bioinformatics

    Nextflow and nf-core

    • Nextflow: workflow manager.
    • nf-core: community-curated Nextflow pipelines.

    Pipelines are listed on the nf-core website. In this workshop we use:

    • nf-core/taxprofiler
    • nf-core/funcprofiler

    Connecting to Nectar

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    Loading the software

    Check that each tool is available:

    BASH 

    java -version
nextflow -version
apptainer --version
nf-core --version

    Preparing the samplesheet

    Both pipelines use the same samplesheet columns: sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta. Paths must be absolute.

    BASH 

    mkdir -p ~/mbite/run && cd ~/mbite/run

echo "sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta" > samplesheet.csv
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  echo "gut${i},run1,ILLUMINA,$HOME/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample${i}.left.fq.gz,$HOME/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample${i}.right.fq.gz," >> samplesheet.csv
done
cat samplesheet.csv

    OUTPUT 

    sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta
gut1,run1,ILLUMINA,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample1.left.fq.gz,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample1.right.fq.gz,
gut2,run1,ILLUMINA,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample2.left.fq.gz,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample2.right.fq.gz,
gut3,run1,ILLUMINA,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample3.left.fq.gz,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample3.right.fq.gz,
gut4,run1,ILLUMINA,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample4.left.fq.gz,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample4.right.fq.gz,
gut5,run1,ILLUMINA,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample5.left.fq.gz,/home/ubuntu/mbite/data/raw/Gut_sample5.right.fq.gz,

    Check that every file listed exists:

    BASH 

    tail -n +2 samplesheet.csv | cut -d, -f4,5 | tr ',' '\n' | xargs ls -l

    Preparing the database sheets

    taxprofiler: databases_taxprofiler.csv

    Columns are tool,db_name,db_params,db_type,db_path.

    BASH 

    cat > databases_taxprofiler.csv << 'EOF'
tool,db_name,db_params,db_type,db_path
kraken2,k2_standard_08gb,,short,/data/databases/kraken2/k2_standard_08gb
bracken,k2_standard_08gb,;-r 150,short,/data/databases/kraken2/k2_standard_08gb
metaphlan,mpa_vJun23,,short,/data/databases/metaphlan/mpa_vJun23_CHOCOPhlAnSGB_202403
motus,motus_db,,short,/data/databases/motus/db_mOTU
sylph,gtdb_r220,,short,/data/databases/sylph/gtdb-r220-c200-dbv1.syldb
EOF

    funcprofiler: databases_funcprofiler.csv

    Columns are tool,db_name,db_entity,db_params,db_path. HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper need one row per database component.

    BASH 

    cat > databases_funcprofiler.csv << 'EOF'
tool,db_name,db_entity,db_params,db_path
humann_v3,humann_v3_uniref90,humann_metaphlan,,/data/databases/humann/metaphlan_vOct22
humann_v3,humann_v3_uniref90,humann_nucleotide,,/data/databases/humann/chocophlan
humann_v3,humann_v3_uniref90,humann_protein,,/data/databases/humann/uniref90_diamond
humann_v3,humann_v3_uniref90,humann_utility,,/data/databases/humann/utility_mapping
eggnogmapper,eggnog_v5,eggnogmapper_db,diamond,/data/databases/eggnog/eggnog_proteins.dmnd
eggnogmapper,eggnog_v5,eggnogmapper_data_dir,,/data/databases/eggnog/data
EOF

    Reproducible launch commands

    Parameters go in a params.json file and the command in a launch script.

    BASH 

    cat > params_taxprofiler.json << EOF
{
  "input": "$HOME/mbite/run/samplesheet.csv",
  "databases": "$HOME/mbite/run/databases_taxprofiler.csv",
  "outdir": "$HOME/mbite/results/taxprofiler",
  "perform_shortread_qc": true,
  "save_analysis_ready_fastqs": true,
  "run_kraken2": true,
  "run_bracken": true,
  "run_metaphlan": true,
  "run_motus": true,
  "run_sylph": true,
  "run_profile_standardisation": true,
  "run_krona": true,
  "taxpasta_add_name": true,
  "taxpasta_add_rank": true,
  "taxpasta_add_lineage": true
}
EOF

    BASH 

    cat > nextflow_launch.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
nextflow run nf-core/taxprofiler \
  -r <version> \
  -profile singularity \
  -params-file params_taxprofiler.json \
  -resume
EOF
chmod +x nextflow_launch.sh

    Alternatively, the nf-core tools launcher writes a nf-params.json interactively:

    BASH 

    nf-core pipelines launch nf-core/taxprofiler -r <version>
    Key Points
    • Pin pipeline versions with -r.
    • Check software with nextflow -version and apptainer --version before launching.
    • Both pipelines need a samplesheet with absolute paths and a database sheet.
    • Keep parameters in params.json and the command in a launch script.

    Content from Taxonomic profiling with nf-core/taxprofiler

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 70 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I configure and run nf-core/taxprofiler?
    • How do sylph, mOTUs, Kraken2/Bracken and MetaPhlAn differ?
    • How do I interpret the pipeline outputs?
    • Which table do I need for downstream analysis in R?

    Objectives

    • Configure taxonomic profiling with nf-core/taxprofiler
    • Explain the roles of sylph, mOTUs, Kraken2/Bracken and MetaPhlAn
    • Interpret the MultiQC report, classification summaries and pipeline reports
    • Identify the standardised abundance table needed for downstream analysis

    The profilers

    • Kraken2 and Bracken
    • MetaPhlAn
    • mOTUs
    • sylph

    Running the pipeline

    BASH 

    cd ~/mbite/run
./nextflow_launch.sh

    or directly:

    BASH 

    nextflow run nf-core/taxprofiler \
  -r 2.0.1 \
  -profile singularity \
  --input samplesheet.csv \
  --databases databases_taxprofiler.csv \
  --outdir ~/mbite/results/taxprofiler \
  --perform_shortread_qc \
  --save_analysis_ready_fastqs \
  --run_kraken2 --run_bracken \
  --run_metaphlan --run_motus --run_sylph \
  --run_profile_standardisation \
  --taxpasta_add_name --taxpasta_add_rank --taxpasta_add_lineage \
  --run_krona \
  -resume

    Output overview

    BASH 

    ls ~/mbite/results/taxprofiler

    OUTPUT 

    analysis_ready_fastqs  bracken  fastp  kraken2  krona  metaphlan  motus
multiqc  pipeline_info  sylph  taxpasta  ...

    MultiQC report

    multiqc/multiqc_report.html contains the read QC (fastp) and classification summaries. Copy it to your laptop to open it:

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    Taxonomic classification summaries

    Standardised and merged tables (Taxpasta)

    Taxpasta converts the output of each profiler into one merged table per profiler and database, with taxa in rows and samples in columns. The tables are in taxpasta/.

    BASH 

    ls ~/mbite/results/taxprofiler/taxpasta/
head -n 5 ~/mbite/results/taxprofiler/taxpasta/bracken_k2_standard_08gb.tsv

    We import these tables into R in the episode Importing and exploring microbiome data with R.

    Pipeline execution and resource reports

    pipeline_info/ contains the execution report, timeline, trace and software versions.

    Key Points
    • nf-core/taxprofiler runs several profilers on the same pre-processed reads.
    • The Taxpasta tables are the input for the analysis in R.
    • pipeline_info/ records resource usage and software versions.

    Content from Functional profiling with nf-core/funcprofiler

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I configure and run nf-core/funcprofiler?
    • What do HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper measure?
    • What is the difference between gene-family abundance, pathway abundance and pathway coverage?

    Objectives

    • Configure functional profiling with nf-core/funcprofiler
    • Explain the roles of HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper
    • Distinguish gene-family abundance, pathway abundance and pathway coverage
    • Identify the standardised function tables needed for downstream analysis

    HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper

    • HUMAnN
    • eggNOG-mapper

    Input: pre-processed reads

    nf-core/funcprofiler does not perform read QC or host removal. We use the reads saved by taxprofiler with --save_analysis_ready_fastqs.

    BASH 

    cd ~/mbite/run
ls ~/mbite/results/taxprofiler/analysis_ready_fastqs/

    BASH 

    READS=~/mbite/results/taxprofiler/analysis_ready_fastqs
echo "sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta" > samplesheet_func.csv
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  r1=$(ls $READS/gut${i}_*_1.fastq.gz)
  r2=$(ls $READS/gut${i}_*_2.fastq.gz)
  echo "gut${i},run1,ILLUMINA,${r1},${r2}," >> samplesheet_func.csv
done
cat samplesheet_func.csv

    Running the pipeline

    BASH 

    nextflow run nf-core/funcprofiler \
  -r <version> \
  -profile singularity \
  --input samplesheet_func.csv \
  --databases databases_funcprofiler.csv \
  --outdir ~/mbite/results/funcprofiler \
  --run_humann_v3 \
  --run_eggnogmapper \
  -resume

    Outputs

    BASH 

    ls ~/mbite/results/funcprofiler
ls ~/mbite/results/funcprofiler/humann_v3/gut1
    • MultiQC report: multiqc/multiqc_report.html
    • Gene family abundance: humann_v3/<sample>/*_genefamilies.tsv
    • Pathway abundance: humann_v3/<sample>/*_pathabundance.tsv
    • Pathway coverage: humann_v3/<sample>/*_pathcoverage.tsv
    • Species functional profiles: stratified rows in the HUMAnN tables
    • eggNOG-mapper annotations: eggnogmapper/<db_name>/*.emapper.annotations
    • Execution and resource reports: pipeline_info/

    BASH 

    head -n 5 ~/mbite/results/funcprofiler/humann_v3/gut1/*_pathabundance.tsv
    Key Points
    • nf-core/funcprofiler expects reads that have already been through QC.
    • HUMAnN reports gene families, pathway abundance and pathway coverage, overall and per species.

    Content from Importing and exploring microbiome data with R

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Which R data structures are used for microbiome data?
    • How do I import Taxpasta and HUMAnN tables and sample metadata into R?
    • How do I filter, aggregate and transform microbiome data?

    Objectives

    • Identify the phyloseq and TreeSummarizedExperiment object types and explain their principal differences
    • Import taxonomic and functional tables and sample metadata
    • Build a TreeSummarizedExperiment object
    • Filter low-prevalence features, aggregate taxa at a selected rank and calculate relative abundance

    Loading the libraries

    Install the packages first (see Setup), then load them:

    R 

    library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(TreeSummarizedExperiment)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)

    Check the versions you are using:

    R 

    packageVersion("mia")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '1.20.0'

    R 

    packageVersion("miaViz")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '1.20.0'

    R 

    packageVersion("TreeSummarizedExperiment")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '2.20.0'

    phyloseq and TreeSummarizedExperiment

    • phyloseq: otu_table, tax_table, sample_data, phy_tree
    • TreeSummarizedExperiment: assay (one or more), rowData, colData, rowTree
    • Convert between them with mia::convertToPhyloseq() and mia::convertFromPhyloseq()

    Importing the data

    Copy the results from Nectar to your laptop (run on your laptop):

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    Sample metadata

    R 

    meta <- read_tsv(meta_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
meta

    Taxonomic table (Taxpasta)

    R 

    tax_tbl <- read_tsv(tax_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
head(tax_tbl)

    Building a TreeSummarizedExperiment

    R 

    annot_cols <- c("taxonomy_id", "name", "rank", "lineage")
sample_cols <- setdiff(colnames(tax_tbl), annot_cols)

counts <- as.matrix(tax_tbl[, sample_cols])
rownames(counts) <- tax_tbl$taxonomy_id

row_df <- tax_tbl |>
  select(any_of(annot_cols)) |>
  separate_wider_delim(lineage, delim = ";",
                       names = c("Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order",
                                 "Family", "Genus", "Species"),
                       too_few = "align_start", too_many = "drop") |>
  as.data.frame()
rownames(row_df) <- tax_tbl$taxonomy_id

col_df <- meta |>
  filter(sample %in% sample_cols) |>
  as.data.frame()
rownames(col_df) <- col_df$sample
col_df <- col_df[sample_cols, ]

tse <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
  assays  = list(counts = counts),
  rowData = row_df,
  colData = col_df
)
tse

    Sequencing depth

    R 

    depth <- data.frame(sample = colnames(tse),
                    reads  = colSums(assay(tse, "counts")))
ggplot(depth, aes(x = sample, y = reads)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Classified reads")

    Filtering, aggregating and transforming

    R 

    tse_species <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Species")
tse_species <- subsetByPrevalent(tse_species,
                                 assay.type = "counts",
                                 detection = 10,
                                 prevalence = 0.2)
tse_species <- transformAssay(tse_species,
                              assay.type = "counts",
                              method = "relabundance")
tse_species

    Visualising composition

    R 

    tse_phylum <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Phylum")
tse_phylum <- transformAssay(tse_phylum, assay.type = "counts",
                             method = "relabundance")
plotAbundance(tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance")

    R 

    plotPrevalence(tse_species, assay.type = "relabundance")
    Key Points
    • Load the packages with library() at the start of the session.
    • A TreeSummarizedExperiment holds assays, feature data (rowData) and sample data (colData).
    • Taxpasta tables are read with readr and assembled into a TreeSummarizedExperiment.
    • agglomerateByRank(), subsetByPrevalent() and transformAssay() aggregate, filter and transform the data.
